introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 3 (0760), Paper 3 - Africa and World History, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2021. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections (Section A: Africa, 1800-1945; Section B: Africa, 1945 to the present; Section C: World Revolutions and Diplomacy, 1700-1919; Section D: World, 1919 to the present date). All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : le sujet impose « answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections ». `regles_choix` porte une règle « 1 sur 3 » par section (A, B, C, D), ce qui correspond exactement à la consigne imprimée ; la consigne complète est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`.

Points : chaque question porte 25 marks imprimés (« All questions carry equal marks »), soit 100 points pour les quatre questions à traiter. Aucun écart de points constaté ; `points` vaut 25 pour l'exercice et pour l'unique question de chaque fichier.

Sujet scanné de deux pages (page de garde et questions 1 à 12) ; publicités, filigranes gcerevision.com et mention manuscrite d'adresse web ignorés ; aucune question coupée ni illisible, aucune figure ni carte dans le sujet.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées au niveau Advanced Level (introduction, développement, conclusion argumentée). Aucune statistique ni citation n'est avancée ; les effectifs sont donnés en ordres de grandeur prudents (« roughly nine to ten million », « about two million »).

Question 2 : l'énoncé imprimé associe « the Jihad in Futa Jallon » aux dates 1854-1864. Ces dates correspondent à la guerre sainte d'Al-Hajj Umar Tall (empire toucouleur, parti de Dinguiraye, en bordure du Fouta-Djalon), alors que le jihad du Fouta-Djalon proprement dit date d'environ 1725 (Karamoko Alfa). Le sujet est recopié tel quel ; le corrigé signale la divergence et traite le mouvement de 1854-1864, avec le jihad du Fouta-Djalon en arrière-plan. L'année de début de la guerre sainte d'Umar est donnée de façon prudente (1852 ou 1854 selon les sources).

Question 2 : détails à vérifier par un historien (siège de Médine en 1857, prise de Ségou en 1861 et de Hamdallahi en 1862, mort d'Umar en 1864, chute de Ségou face à Archinard en 1890) ; ils sont cités conformément à l'historiographie courante, mais le corrigé ne s'appuie pas sur des chiffres.

Question 7 : les dates de 1688 sont données en style ancien (naissance du prince le 10 juin, invitation des « Immortal Seven » et acquittement des sept évêques le 30 juin, débarquement à Torbay le 5 novembre) ; le corrigé précise le choix du calendrier julien.
Question 4 : le massacre de Thiaroye (décembre 1944), les émeutes d'Accra (1948) et la conférence de Brazzaville (1944) sont cités sans bilan chiffré, le nombre exact de victimes étant discuté.

Question 5 : exemples de coups d'État (Togo 1963, Ghana 1966, Nigeria 1966, Ouganda 1971, Éthiopie 1974, Mali 2020) cités sans chiffres ; la formule « very many people were killed » remplace volontairement tout bilan sous Amin, très discuté.

Question 12 : la liste des suspensions et départs (Nigeria 1995, Fidji, Zimbabwe 2003, Gambie 2013 puis retour 2018) et l'adhésion du Cameroun en 1995 sont citées de mémoire historique ; aucun chiffre financier n'est avancé.

Questions à thème régional : les noms de thèmes sont qualifiés (par exemple `military coups in africa`, `refugee crisis in africa`, `league of nations`) pour éviter les collisions avec les Tags de l'Histoire francophone ; à reverifier à l'ingestion avec `find_tag_variant`.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Evaluate the consequences of the First World War.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The First World War (1914-1918) involved the Allied and Associated Powers (including Britain, France, Russia until 1917, Italy and later the United States) against the Central Powers (Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria). It was the first total war, with large numbers of soldiers and civilians involved and an extensive use of new weapons. Its consequences were political, territorial, economic, social and international, and they were partly the cause of the Second World War. The most important consequences were the political and territorial changes in Europe and the weakening of Europe in the world.

**1. Human and social consequences.**
- Roughly nine to ten million soldiers died and about twice as many were wounded; large numbers of civilians died from hunger, disease and violence. Millions of people were disabled or displaced; there were many refugees.
- Society changed: women had worked in industry and agriculture and won the vote in many countries (for example in Britain in 1918 for women over thirty, in Germany in 1919 and in the United States in 1920). Class relations, trade unions and attitudes to authority changed. A generation of young men was lost in many countries.

**2. Political and territorial consequences.**
- *Collapse of empires.* Four empires disappeared: Russia (the Tsar fell in 1917), Germany (the Kaiser abdicated in November 1918), Austria-Hungary (broken up in 1918) and the Ottoman Empire (replaced by the Turkish Republic in 1923).
- *New states.* Poland, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia (the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes), Austria, Hungary, Finland and the Baltic states appeared in Europe, following the principle of self-determination, though many minorities remained and became sources of conflict.
- *The peace settlements.* The Treaty of Versailles (28 June 1919) forced Germany to accept responsibility for the war (Article 231), pay reparations, limit its army to 100,000 men, give up territory (Alsace-Lorraine to France, land to Poland, and all of its colonies) and accept the demilitarisation of the Rhineland. The treaties of Saint-Germain, Trianon, Neuilly and Sevres dealt with the other Central Powers. German resentment of the "Diktat" helped extremists such as Hitler.
- *Revolution.* The Bolshevik Revolution of 1917 and the creation of a communist state, the Soviet Union, started an ideological conflict that was important for the rest of the century. Fear of communism helped the rise of fascism in Italy (1922) and later of Nazism in Germany.
- *New international order.* The League of Nations was created in 1920 to maintain peace through collective security, though it was weakened by the absence of the United States and others.

**3. Economic consequences.** Europe was heavily damaged and indebted; Britain and France owed large debts to the United States, which became the leading creditor and financial power. Reparations and war debts caused tension and instability; Germany suffered the hyperinflation of 1923; economic disruption and the later Great Depression of 1929 had links with the war's legacy.

**4. Consequences outside Europe, including Africa.** Germany's colonies were taken over as mandates of the League of Nations (under Article 22 of the Covenant), classified according to their stage of development. German Cameroon, already occupied by British and French forces in 1914-1916, was divided between Britain and France in 1916, and the mandates were confirmed in 1922. African soldiers and carriers had served in the war and many returned with new ideas, and the war encouraged nationalism and anti-colonial movements, in the Arab world, India and Africa. Japan and the United States became stronger.

**5. Evaluation.** The most important consequences were the political and territorial changes, since they created the instability and resentments behind the Second World War, together with the decline of European power and the rise of the United States and the Soviet Union. Some consequences, such as the achievements of women or the League's creation, were more positive, but the overall effect was destructive.

**Conclusion.** The First World War changed the map of Europe, destroyed four empires, produced a harsh and unstable peace, started the communist era, strengthened nationalism and weakened Europe's world position. Its consequences were largely negative and led directly to the next world war.
